In nailing, the nails themselves are the support.
The slabs follow each other about every 3,5 m.
Only the embedment holds it – no anchor, no strut.
A trench is a narrow excavation whose width is typically at most 1–3 m, made mostly for linear works (e.g. utilities).
Temporary: it is backfilled once the utility is complete.
In coarse-grained, cohesionless soil a vertical soil face temporarily stands without support down to 1–2 m.
In coarse-grained soil (without apparent cohesion) m₀ = 0 – so pre-driven (steel) planking is needed there.
In cohesionless granular soil the slope angle cannot be greater than the angle of internal friction of the soil.
For a higher slope (above 3–5 m) it is also advisable to build a berm.
Above the slope, within the failure plane, we can safely stockpile the excavated soil, since a surface load of 10 kPa is assumed in design anyway.
It is advisable to specify that nothing is stockpiled within the failure plane; the minimum 10 kPa load only covers the usual variable load.
Shoring means “bracing one side against the other”: the pressure of the two opposite soil faces is taken by struts in compression.
So as the excavation gets wider, the buckling length of the struts – and the danger of buckling – grows.
In traditional timber shoring the struts were typically round timbers 30–40 cm in diameter.
The struts were round timbers 12–16 cm in diameter, the planks were 2 inches (48 mm) thick, and the walings were beams of 12–24 cm side length.
In hard clay, for occupational safety, shoring is needed from a depth of 0,5 m.
Shoring is needed for H > 0,5 m in fine sand, H > 1,0 m in intermediate soil and H > 2,0 m in hard clay.
If m₀ > H, vertical planking can be used: the excavation is dug to full depth, then the faces are lined and strutted.
If H > m₀: stepwise driven planking; if H ≫ m₀: horizontal planking with excavation in steps; if m₀ = 0: pre-driven planking.
In pre-driven planking timber planks can also be used, since they are driven before excavation.
Pre-driven planking is made of steel only – the sheets are driven or vibrated in, and only then is the soil dug out.
The advantage of horizontal planking is that the length of the planks is not limited, and they are not damaged during installation, since they do not have to be driven.
It is used when H ≫ m₀, and m₀ is only of the order of decimetres.
In medium- and high-plasticity soil the strut pressure is the smaller of p₁ = (H·γn + q) − 4c and p₂ = 0,2·(H·γn + q).
The greater of the two has to be taken into account.
In an excavation wider than about 3 m, buckling of the struts already has to be considered.
Then bracing in several directions, raking struts or large-diameter steel tubular struts are needed.
In a wide excavation the raking struts can also bear on the inner part of the base slab built in advance.
At the edge a sloping soil support (earth berm) is then left, which is later removed in sections.
The soldier pile wall is watertight, so it is an economical solution even with high groundwater.
A solution for dry excavations without groundwater: water seeps through between the planks.
The steel soldiers of a soldier pile wall are typically placed 4–6 m apart.
Every 1–3 m, usually 2 m apart; a closer spacing can be justified by higher loads.
In a jet grout wall the size of the steel member can be increased at will, in proportion to the diameter of the jet column.
The fresh jetted soil is a dense fluid: only the vertical line passed through by the drill rod and its 15–20 cm surroundings will accept the steel member.
If the spacing of the jet columns is 10–20 cm smaller than their diameter, the wall can be quasi-watertight.
This is its great advantage over the traditional soldier pile wall.
In the reinforced self-hardening slurry wall, after grab excavation and placing the steel beams, concrete replaces the slurry.
No concrete replaces the slurry: the cement-bearing slurry itself hardens and gives the wall its watertightness.
The 28-day compressive strength of self-hardening slurry is typically 0,5–1,4 MPa.
The load is carried by steel sections placed every 1–2 m; by arching, the slurry transfers the earth and water pressure to them.
Thanks to the interlocks of steel sheet piles a watertight wall can be made, and for a temporary wall the piles can be extracted.
A sheet pile wall can be temporary or permanent; for permanent use there are separate corrosion protection requirements.
The vibrations from driving sheet piles reach only 2–3 m, so they need not be considered in built-up areas.
The vibrations can reach as far as 20–30 m – it has to be checked whether they could damage the surrounding buildings.
Reinforced concrete sheet piles are used mainly for temporary excavations, because they are easy to extract.
They are used for permanent sheeting, mainly in harbours, open water and bank protection. They are heavy, and hard to drive too (water jetting helps).
In Hungary the plastic sheet pile wall is the most widespread type of sheet pile wall.
It is not yet widespread in Hungary; steel sheet piles (Larssen and Hoesch types) are used most often.
In a secant pile wall every pile is reinforced, and the reinforced piles are made first.
Only every second pile is reinforced. First the unreinforced (primary) piles are made, then the reinforced ones between them, cutting about 10–12 cm into them.
In a spaced pile wall the gap between piles is typically 20–60 cm, but at most equal to the pile diameter.
The acceptable gap depends on the stability of the soil and its ability to arch.
In Hungary pile walls are popular mainly as non-watertight excavation support walls above the groundwater level.
They are most often made with CFA technology; in Hungary mainly the spaced form has spread.
In soil nailing the excavation is deepened in vertical sections of 90–180 cm, depending on the stability of the soil.
In each lift: nails, steel mesh, shotcrete – then excavation of the next section.
The required length of soil nails is typically 0,1–0,3 times the excavation depth.
For an excavation of depth H, the nail length is 0,6–1,2·H depending on the soil; the grid is typically 0,5–1,0 (1,5) m.
Soil nailing can also be used well in soft, plastic clay and organic soil.
It cannot be used in soft, plastic clay, organic soil, rubble fill or bouldery soil.
Cantilever excavation supports (without other support) are typically stable only to an excavation depth of about 4–6 m.
And only if there is no structure right beside them. For a deeper excavation they have to be supported at one or more levels.
Like a soil nail, a ground anchor transfers the force to the soil along its whole length.
The anchor transfers force only along its fixed (grouted) length; the free length only carries it between the head and the fixed length.
The fixed length of a ground anchor has to extend beyond the active slip surface.
Otherwise the anchor would move together with the sliding soil mass.
In Hungary drilled, grouted ground anchors are almost always temporary, with a design life of at most 2 years.
Permanent anchors can also be made, with stricter corrosion protection and the possibility of re-stressing.
After hardening, anchors are prestressed to 120–130% of the design load.
After hardening (8–12 days) they are prestressed to 80–90% of the design load, and a test load record is made for every anchor.
The shortest ground anchor is about 8 m long, because both the free and the fixed length are at least 4 m.
Typical inclination 15–30°, length at most 25–30 m, fixed length 4–9 m, 3–7 strands.
For steel tubular struts longer than 10–15 m, the axial compressive forces from thermal expansion already govern.
The strut has to be designed for them too; the tubes are typically made of S235–S355 steel, 30–150 cm in diameter.
In the top-down (Milan) method the slabs can be cast on the ground, without falsework.
Further advantages are the great stiffness of the slab supports and the shorter construction time.
In top-down construction the excavation takes place above the completed supporting slab, in the open air.
The excavation proceeds under the supporting slab, in a confined space – ventilation and lighting have to be provided.
In a passive tieback, because there is no prestress, the movements of the wall are larger, typically a few centimetres.
The wall is tied to a structure (a wall or a row of piles) located far enough behind the retained soil mass.
A frozen wall forms faster with liquid nitrogen than with brine cooling.
With nitrogen (−196 °C) about 1–3 weeks, with brine (about −30 °C) about 4–8 weeks – but nitrogen is expensive, so the wall is often maintained with brine.
The (vertical or horizontal) element lining the soil face – formerly 48 mm timber, today mostly steel trench sheets.
The beam (timber or steel I/U section) holding the planks together, at right angles to them; the struts bear on it.
A compression member bracing the opposite soil faces against each other (round timber, I-beam, tube, steel screw strut).
m₀ (unsupported depth)
The depth to which a vertical soil face above the groundwater temporarily stands without support: m₀ = 4c/(nγ)·tan(45°+φ/2) − p/γ.
trench sheet (Patria, Union)
Thin-walled profiled steel sheet for lining trenches – its joints are not watertight.
vertical / stepwise driven / horizontal / pre-driven planking
The four planking methods, by the relationship between m₀ and H.
strut pressure
The equivalent horizontal load acting on the shoring, assumed uniform (the reaction of the preloaded struts).
A reusable shoring frame of prefabricated, stiffened steel panels and adjustable struts.
raking strut
In a wide excavation, an inclined member supporting the wall on the bottom of the excavation or on the base slab; its vertical equilibrium also has to be checked.
A soil support left beside the wall, which holds the wall by its passive resistance until the raking struts are installed.
soldier pile (Siemens) wall
Steel I-beams installed in the ground at intervals, with lagging placed between them keeping pace with the excavation.
A soil column mixed in place by a high-pressure cement grout jet (60–120 cm); the element of a jet grout wall.
self-hardening slurry
A bentonite-cement slurry that supports the trench, then hardens itself (0,5–1,4 MPa).
Deep mixing methods: cutter-wheel panels, chain mixer (continuous trench), or intersecting columns.
sheet pile
An element driven, vibrated or pressed into the ground, connected to the next by interlocks (mainly steel: Larssen, Hoesch).
interlock
The connection between sheet piles; it makes the wall continuous and watertight.
spaced / contiguous / secant pile wall
Pile wall layouts: with gaps, with touching piles, or with piles drilled into each other (the last one watertight).
primary / secondary pile
In a secant wall, first the unreinforced (primary) piles are made, then the reinforced (secondary) piles between them, cutting into them.
A reinforced concrete beam tying together the tops of the piles (wall elements) – the supports can also connect to it.
At a deeper level, a load-spreading beam fixed to the side of the wall, to which anchors or tubular struts connect.
A reinforcing bar, typically 20–28 mm, driven or drilled and grouted into the soil face; it works along its whole length.
shotcrete
Concrete sprayed onto the face (8–15 (20) cm in nailing, with steel mesh).
The structure transferring the anchor force to the wall: bearing plate, locking element (wedge, nut).
The part of the anchor between the head and the fixed length – it slides in a sheath and transfers no force to the soil.
The grouted body of the anchor (typically 4–9 m), which transfers the force to the soil beyond the active slip surface.
strand
High-strength steel strand; typically 3–7 in one anchor.
prestressing
Tensioning the anchor after hardening to 80–90% of the design load, then locking it at the head.
active slip surface (failure plane)
The boundary of the soil wedge behind the wall that tends to slide; the fixed lengths of the anchors and the stockpiles should be outside it.
A large-diameter (30–150 cm) steel tube bracing opposite walls against each other – it also has to be designed for thermal expansion.
top-down (Milan) method
First the retaining walls and the top slab are built, and the excavation proceeds downwards under the slabs.
passive anchor
An untensioned tie to a wall or row of piles set further back, outside the failure plane.
An outer pipe closed at the bottom with a down-pipe inside; the coolant (brine or liquid nitrogen) circulates in it.
brine
A calcium chloride solution, cooled by a refrigeration plant to about −25…−40 °C and circulated in a closed loop in the freeze pipes.
cellular cofferdam
Steel cells of straight-web sheet piles filled with sand – a self-supporting gravity structure in open water.
tremie method
Underwater concreting through a pipe in such a way that the end of the pipe stays in the fresh concrete throughout.
The upward lifting effect of water pressure on the bottom of the excavation; it is resisted by weight and/or tension piles (anchors).
